+# Acceptance Criteria
+
+Rules:
+
+- Criteria lines use the exact format `- ACn: <criterion>`.
+- Every criterion ends with [verify: exec `<command>`],
+  [verify: invariant `<command>`], [verify: judged] or
+  [verify: none — <reason>].
+- After `flow freeze` this file is checksum-protected: any edit outside
+  `keryx flow ac update` fails every gate and status transition.
+- Completion requires every ACn to be confirmed via
+  `keryx flow ac confirm <id> <ACn>`.
+
+## Criteria
+
+- AC1: `keryx review ingest --premises <file|->` reads a premise claims file (context.md "Contract") and merges it delete-only after dedupe: `upheld` changes nothing; `downgraded` lowers severity (a raise is rejected); `challenged`/`owner-decision` mark the finding held; claims with an unknown finding id, a judge equal to the finding's reporter, `challenged` without an intent signal or practice source, or a held verdict without a question (owner-decision without ≥2 options) are rejected and listed in scope.md; the claims are stored in `research-evidence/premises.json` and on each finding record. Tests per rule. · sensitive: failure-scenario [verify: exec `bun test src/review/premise.test.ts`]
+- AC2: A held finding is not counted as an open blocker/major by the verdict, is listed as "awaiting operator: <ids>", and readiness and the flow review gate fail while any held finding has no operator decision; a downgraded severity is the one verdict and dedupe use. Tests. [verify: exec `bun test src/review/verdict.test.ts src/review/readiness.test.ts src/flow/review-gate.test.ts src/review/dedupe.test.ts`]
+- AC3: Operator decision kind `premise-question`: `keryx review decide-premise --package <dir> --finding <id> --answer uphold|dismiss --reason "<why>"` needs a terminal (refused in the no-prompt routine list) and has a keryx shell card `review_decide_premise`; `uphold` returns the finding to kept at its original severity, `dismiss` records `dismissed-incorrect` with the operator's reason; after it, readiness and the gate pass for that finding. Tests. [verify: exec `bun test src/review/premise-decision.test.ts src/commands/review-operator-cli.test.ts src/commands/operator-confirm-review-tools.test.ts`]
+- AC4: `review-premise` is a bundled reviewer (catalog, install manifest, both skill copies byte-identical, length ceiling set, `model_tier: deep`, not in the fan-out roster, never path-gated, iron-laws and class-scope exemptions with reasons, `keryx review tier` gives it deep); its SKILL.md requires claim-first reading (the finding's claim before the reviewer's argument), the four questions (intent, accepted practice, consistency, fix soundness), cited signals or sources for `challenged`, and delete-only output. [verify: invariant `bun test src/gdskills/ src/review/coverage.test.ts src/commands/skills.bundled-verify.test.ts`]
+- AC5: Every reviewer carries a fourth shared law, from the canonical block: an explicit override, suppression, exemption, a comment or commit giving a reason, or a sibling doing the same is a deliberate choice, not a defect until its reason is read and shown wrong; a project rule is checked against accepted platform practice and its known exceptions before a deviation from it is reported. review-layout's RTL section names what does not mirror (media/playback controls and progress, timelines, numbers and code, charts' time axes unless the product decides otherwise). [verify: invariant `bun test src/gdskills/review-skills-iron-laws.test.ts src/gdskills/`]
+- AC6: review-orchestrator runs `review-premise` as Wave D after the verifier over the canonical findings (severity ≥ minor; in a delta round only those without a carried premise), passes its result with `--premises`, and stays within its length ceiling. flow-orchestrator, job-orchestrator, review-pr-feedback and feature-dev never pass a held finding in `fix_context.review_feedback`; they ask the operator (card in keryx shell, question tool elsewhere) and record the answer with `review decide-premise`; a flow whose source is a follow-up issue or an external review finding runs `review-premise` on it before freeze. Both copies identical. [verify: invariant `bun test src/gdskills/`]
+- AC7: Evaluation (live, Opus): on a synthetic fixture reproducing the #7849 case (explicit `dir="ltr"` on a playback timeline, an exemption note, a sibling media control doing the same) `review-premise` returns `challenged` or `owner-decision` for the "timeline pinned LTR" finding, citing an intent signal and a platform practice source; on the round-2 ground-truth findings of #992 and #1005 (and the fixture's real control findings) it challenges none. Results and dispatch/token counts in `eval/`. [verify: judged]
+- AC8: The repository stays green (CI) and a patch release containing this flow is published to npm. [verify: exec `npm view @mrciphersmith/keryx version`]

+1. [2.081] Findings reach a review round through the report's keryx:findings block, and a round without one silently records none (known-mistake/accepted) - known-mistakes/review-ingest-discards-verdicts.md
+   `keryx review ingest --report <md>` reads structured findings from a fenced ` ```json keryx:findings ` block inside the report. A report without that block ingests as `findings: in=0`, and every `--verifications` claim naming one of its findings is then discarded as unresolvable — because the finding it names is not in the round.

+2. [1.841] Theme switch repaints already-rendered chrome via old-slot value matching (lesson/accepted) - lessons/theme-switch-repaint.md
+   `/theme` in the OpenTUI shell applied and persisted correctly on 0.2.66, but `applyTheme` (src/tui/shell-chrome.ts) only recolored the chrome's OWN surfaces (renderer background, sidebar border, docks, composer, `/`-menu). Every renderable painted EARLIER with `getTheme()` — transcript frames (user echoes, code-segment boxes, block bodies, side-worker boxes), tone-colored block headers (`theme.error`/`theme.tool`), dock/queue-dock buttons, sidebar panels — kept the old palette's hex in its `borderColor`/`backgroundColor`/`fg` props, so a dark→dark switch (groknight↔tokyonight) looked like "the theme did not apply". Fix: on every `applyTheme`, walk the renderable trees (transcript, docks, sidebarTop, menu, composer, header, footer) and rewrite any prop whose color equals an OLD theme slot hex to the NEW slot hex.

+## Agent Findings
+
+### Case (vantage-frontend #7849 → #7908 → #7966)
+
+- Finding (final review of #7435): "Playback slider pinned LTR — `MultiLayerPlaybackSlider.tsx:150` and `PlaybackHeader.tsx:101` hard-code `dir="ltr"`, so the timeline does not mirror in RTL." Filed as an issue item, implemented in #7908, extracted to #7966, reviewed twice (implementation only), approved, then refuted by the owner on platform practice (Material: do not mirror media controls/progress; Apple HIG: video controls and timeline indicators do not flip) and closed.
+- Intent signals present in the code and ignored: explicit `dir="ltr"` override; a lint exemption noted as a "physical-LTR scroll/pixel island"; `MediaPlaybackControls.tsx:81` also forces `dir="ltr"`. The fix's reviewer filed that sibling as a follow-up instead of as evidence against the premise.
+- The finding travelled through a follow-up ISSUE, not a review round: a premise check only inside `review ingest` would not have caught the implementation step.
+
+### Where the gap is (0.3.120)
+
+- Shared laws: canonical block `review-orchestrator/SKILL.md` "### Shared laws (every reviewer)" (~1318), copied into every reviewer, enforced by `src/gdskills/review-skills-iron-laws.test.ts` (derived from the canonical block; EXEMPT map 45-56). Laws: no reproducible path → info; never the theoretical; one per class. No intent/practice law.
+- `review-layout/SKILL.md:116-124` RTL section lists only what flips.
+- `review-verifier/SKILL.md:127` confirmed = procedure reproduced the defect; the verifier is delete-only (`src/review/verification.ts:173`).
+
+### Wiring map for a new delete-only judge (mirror the verifier)
+
+- types: `src/review/types.ts` verification vocab 287-379, finding `verification?` 479, managed input 594-604, package counts 784-787.
+- merge: `src/review/verification.ts` (claims 143, merge 173, self-verification rejection, scope.md render 578-605).
+- ingest: `src/commands/review.ts` flags 331/333, managed input 1049, reader 3586, counts 1128, help 4784/4865/5256; `src/commands/automatic-review.ts:203` CREATE_PATH_FLAGS; `src/review/managed.ts` merge 306, dedupe 349, persist 1540, scope blocks 2429.
+- verdict `src/review/verdict.ts` classify 115-131, `VERIFICATIONS_FILE` 23; readiness `src/review/readiness.ts` verifierCheck 171, registry 318; flow gate `src/flow/review-gate.ts` 1221/1511-1578, dispositions 590-686.
+- dedupe `src/review/dedupe.ts` severityRule; coverage `NOT_ROSTER` `src/review/coverage.ts:72`; operator decisions `src/review/operator-decisions.ts:17`, `src/commands/review-operator.ts:124`, `src/commands/operator-confirm-review.ts:565`; tier `src/gdskills/model-tier.ts:1337`; routing `src/commands/routing-corpus.ts:399,725,901`; catalog `src/gdskills/catalog.ts:282`; manifest `src/gdskills/bundled/install-manifest.json:474`; ceilings `src/gdskills/skill-length-ceilings.ts` (orchestrator at its 1582 ceiling — offset any new text; ceilings are only lowered).
+- count tests: `src/gdskills/bundled-eval.test.ts:119` (79), `src/commands/skills.bundled-verify.test.ts:40-52` (79); exempt lists in the iron-laws and class-scope tests.
+- fix-loop consumers: flow-orchestrator SKILL.md 412/447/690, task-implementer `input-contract.schema.json:140` `fix_context.review_feedback`, job-orchestrator, review-pr-feedback, feature-dev.
+
+### Contract (all lanes build to this)
+
+Premise claims file, `--premises <file|->` on `keryx review ingest` (beside `--verifications`):
+
+```json
+{ "judge": "review-premise", "model": "<id>",
+  "premises": [ {
+    "finding_id": "LY-003",
+    "verdict": "upheld | downgraded | challenged | owner-decision",
+    "severity": "minor",
+    "intent_signals": [ { "ref": "src/x.tsx:150 | <sha>", "says": "explicit dir=ltr override" } ],
+    "practice_sources": [ { "name": "Material Design — Bidirectionality", "says": "media controls do not mirror" } ],
+    "reasoning": "…",
+    "question": "…",
+    "options": ["uphold — mirror the timeline", "dismiss — keep LTR, as platforms do"]
+  } ] }
+```
+
+- `severity` only with `downgraded`, strictly lower than the finding's. `question` with `challenged`/`owner-decision`; `options` (≥2) with `owner-decision`.
+- Delete-only: never adds a finding, never raises severity, never edits finding text. A judge equal to the finding's reporter is rejected (`self-judgement`). `challenged` needs ≥1 intent_signal or practice_source. An unknown finding id is rejected. Rejections are listed in scope.md like discarded verification claims.
+- Stored at `research-evidence/premises.json`; a `premise` field on each finding record; counts in scope.md.
+- Runs after dedupe over canonical findings of severity ≥ minor; external (PR-comment) findings may be challenged — they become questions, never auto-dismissed. Carried findings in a delta round keep their premise.
+- Effect: `challenged`/`owner-decision` findings are **held** — not counted as open blocker/major, not passed in `fix_context.review_feedback`, listed in the verdict as "awaiting operator: <ids>". Readiness and the flow review gate fail while a held finding has no operator decision.
+- Operator decision kind `premise-question`: `keryx review decide-premise --package <dir> --finding <id> --answer uphold|dismiss --reason "<why>"` (terminal; card `review_decide_premise` in keryx shell, like `review_override_reviewers`). `uphold` returns the finding to kept at its original severity; `dismiss` records `dismissed-incorrect` with the operator's reason as evidence.
+- `downgraded` makes the judge's severity canonical (dedupe and verdict use it).
+- Tier: `review-premise` runs on the deep tier (`model_tier: deep`); `keryx review tier` gives it deep.
+- Standalone use (no review round): `keryx review premise-check --finding-file <json>` is NOT added; a fix-loop orchestrator whose input is a follow-up issue or an external finding dispatches `review-premise` directly with the finding text and code refs, and asks the operator on `challenged`/`owner-decision` before implementing.

+# Review findings get an independent premise check before anyone acts on them
+
+Status: formalized
+Source: owner (origin: human-request)
+
+## Problem
+
+A keryx final review of vantage-frontend #7435 reported "Playback slider pinned LTR": `MultiLayerPlaybackSlider.tsx:150` and `PlaybackHeader.tsx:101` hard-code `dir="ltr"`, so the timeline does not mirror in RTL (issue #7849). The finding was wrong: Material Design and Apple's RTL guidance say media playback controls and timelines do not mirror, and the code carried three signals of a deliberate choice (an explicit `dir="ltr"` override, a lint exemption noted as a "physical-LTR scroll/pixel island", and `MediaPlaybackControls` doing the same). The agent implemented the mirroring (#7908, then #7966); two keryx-style reviews of that fix checked only the implementation (RTL maths, tests, lint) and passed it; a reviewer even noted the inconsistency with `MediaPlaybackControls` and filed it as a follow-up. When a human asked "is this standard practice?", the model refuted the finding at once, and the PR was closed after costing reviewer time and trust.
+
+Verified on 0.3.120:
+- The shared reviewer laws (copied into every reviewer `SKILL.md`, enforced by `src/gdskills/review-skills-iron-laws.test.ts`) cover reachability, no theoretical findings and one finding per class. Nothing tells a reviewer that an explicit override, suppression or exemption is a decision whose reason must be read before calling it a defect, or to check a project rule against accepted platform practice and its known exceptions. The finding passed all three laws: the harm (an LTR timeline in Arabic) is reproducible.
+- `review-layout` § "Logical properties and RTL" lists what must flip and nothing that must not.
+- `review-verifier` confirms a finding when its procedure "reproduced the defect" (`review-verifier/SKILL.md:127`). A fact ("`dir="ltr"` is hard-coded") always reproduces; whether it is a defect at all is asked by no role.
+- A fix round treats the finding's premise as settled: flow-orchestrator treats `suggested_fix` as a hypothesis about HOW, not about WHETHER.
+
+## Expected Outcome
+
+1. Prevention in the reviewers: a fourth shared law — a deliberate choice (explicit override, suppression, exemption, comment or commit giving a reason, a sibling doing the same) is not a defect until its reason is read and shown wrong, and a project rule is checked against accepted platform practice and its known exceptions. `review-layout` names what does not mirror.
+2. An independent final check, `review-premise`: after the verifier, on a clean context and without the reviewer's reasoning first, it judges every finding that asks for a behaviour or structure change on intent, accepted practice (platform guidelines, language idioms, clean code, common patterns), consistency and fix soundness, and returns `upheld | downgraded | challenged | owner-decision`. `challenged` and `owner-decision` findings do not block and are not sent to a fixer; they become operator questions (card in keryx shell, question tool elsewhere).
+3. The same premise check runs in flow-orchestrator (and the other fix-loop orchestrators) before a finding that changes user-visible behaviour is implemented.
+
+## Outcome criteria
+
+- Запрос: «главное нужно понять почему ревьюер нашел ошибку там где ее нет, и почему в пре было неправильное исправление… Можем ли мы для keryx реализовать дополнительного независимого верификатора, который в самом конце перепроверяет находки на логику, смысл, клинкод, и другие обще принятые паттерны? что бы он находил вот такое»; «может это растет изза того что reviewing не достаточно четко описан?» (claude-code session 2026-10-16, after vantage-frontend #7966)
+- Эффект: ложные находки «по правилу, но против практики/намерения» не доходят до исполнителя; вместо неверного фикса оператор получает вопрос.
+- Как наблюдать: на эталоне #7849 (playback LTR) review-premise выдаёт challenged/owner-decision; на наборах реальных находок #992/#1005 он не гасит ни одной подтверждённой; владелец видит то же на следующем PR vantage-frontend.
+
+## Out of Scope
+
+- Changing what each reviewer looks for beyond the shared law and the review-layout "does not mirror" list.
+- Re-opening vantage-frontend #7966/#7908 (owner already closed and reverted).

+# Flow 459 evaluation (AC7)
+
+Live run, judge = `review-premise` on Opus, one fresh subagent per input set, prompt = SKILL.md path + repo path + findings path only.
+
+| Set | Finding | Verdict | Pass |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| fixture (#7849 analogue) | F1 timeline pinned LTR (major) | challenged, 6 intent signals, 2 practice sources (Material, Apple HIG) | yes |
+| fixture | C1 wheel seek ignores scrollLeft | upheld | yes |
+| fixture | C2 resize listener not removed | upheld | yes |
+| fixture | C3 icon-only button, no name | upheld | yes |
+| #1005 @ f5d3385f | F-066 | upheld | yes |
+| #1005 | F-067 | upheld | yes |
+| #992 @ d9ccfb6c | F-007, F-008 | upheld | yes |
+| #992 | F-009, F-011, F-012 | downgraded major -> minor | MISS |
+
+Dispatches 1 per set (3 total). Subagent tokens: fixture 70,419 / #1005 74,684 / #992 80,772.
+All three claims files parse and merge with `parsePremiseClaims` + `mergePremises` (`inputs/validate.ts`, outputs `validate-*.json`): 11 claims applied, 0 rejected.
+
+## Reading
+
+- The headline case works: F1 is held with cited intent and practice, and no real or truth finding is challenged or held (AC7 as worded is met).
+- Strictly (a downgrade of a truth finding is a miss) three of the seven #992/#1005 truth findings were downgraded. All three are test-coverage-gap findings (surviving mutants, no runtime defect) that the judge re-graded minor using the canonical severity rubric. It never held them, so none would be blocked from a fix loop; they only drop out of the major count. Whether that is a defect is an owner call: the downgrade is rubric-consistent, but it is outside the premise-judge's brief (is it a defect at all).
+
+Files: `judge-*.raw.md` (raw outputs), `premise-eval.json`, `validate-*.json`, `inputs/` (findings, validate.ts, fixture.bundle: `git clone` it to reproduce the repo).
+Caveats: the truth findings carry no `title`; the #1005/#992 checkouts contain round-1 review packages (as any real repo would); fixture findings were authored by the evaluator.
+
+## Rerun on #992 after the fix (commit f41a21612)
+
+Fix: a `downgraded` claim needs a cited intent signal or practice source (`downgrade-without-evidence` otherwise); the skill forbids rubric re-grades and its worked example no longer teaches one. Same prompt shape, fresh Opus judge (86,933 subagent tokens), raw output `judge-pr992-rerun.raw.md`.
+
+| Finding | Verdict | Reading |
+|---|---|---|
+| F-007, F-008, F-011 | upheld | pass (F-011 was a rubric downgrade before; fixed) |
+| F-009 | downgraded major -> minor, 2 intent signals (commit d9ccfb6ce, `test-preload-hooks.ts:4`) + 2 practice sources (Bun preload hooks, xUnit fresh fixture) | stays at the fix-loop threshold (minor); the judge argues the reset is deliberate standard isolation and does not hide F-007 "by construction" |
+| F-012 | challenged, held for the operator | the judge argues M10 is an equivalent mutant (every read checks the spelled key, which equals the exact hash for non-shell calls) and that the suggested test cannot kill it; the finding itself said "may be partly equivalent", confidence medium |
+
+Net on 10 controls: 8 upheld, 1 downgraded with cited evidence (still minor, still fixed), 1 held as an operator question (not dismissed). Strict AC7 ("challenges none of the truth findings") is not met for F-012; whether this hold is a defect or the intended behaviour is the owner's judgement (AC7 is `judged`).

+# Implementation Plan
+
+Status: formalized
+
+## Approach
+
+Two layers, because either alone fails on this case:
+
+1. **Prevention in every reviewer** (cheap, runs where the finding is born): a fourth shared law about deliberate choices and accepted practice, propagated through the canonical block, plus a "does not mirror" list in review-layout.
+2. **An independent delete-only judge, `review-premise`** (catches what a rule-anchored reviewer still raises): mirrors the verifier's wiring — claims file, delete-only merge, stored record, verdict/readiness/gate effects — with one new effect, *held* findings that wait for an operator decision instead of reaching a fixer. Clean context and claim-first reading counter anchoring on the reviewer's argument.
+
+The fix-loop orchestrators (flow-orchestrator, job-orchestrator, review-pr-feedback, feature-dev) skip held findings in `fix_context.review_feedback` and ask the operator. A flow whose source is a follow-up issue or an external finding runs `review-premise` on it before planning — that is the path the case actually took.
+
+Alternative rejected: extending `review-verifier`. The verifier runs on the light tier and its value is that it runs something; a premise judgement is the opposite (reasoning on practice and intent, deep tier). Mixing them would cap one by the other's rules (`REASONING_CAPPED_VERDICT`).
+
+State × event matrix: not applicable — CLI/package records and skill text; no UI state. The keryx shell card is an existing card kind (`operator-confirm-review.ts`) with one new decision spec.
+
+## Steps (lanes)
+
+- **L1 code core** (T1): types, `src/review/premise.ts` (claims, validation, delete-only merge), managed ingest after dedupe, persistence, scope.md block, verdict held class, readiness check, flow review-gate condition, dedupe severity, coverage `NOT_ROSTER`. Tests in `src/review/premise.test.ts` + the touched suites.
+- **L2 operator + CLI surface** (T2, after T1): `premise-question` decision kind, `keryx review decide-premise` (terminal + card), `--premises` flag/help/automatic-review path flags, tier rule, routing corpus, catalog + install manifest, docs/cli-reference + review-with-a-record guide.
+- **L3 skills** (T3, parallel with T1): new `review-premise/SKILL.md` (both copies); shared law 4 in the canonical block and every reviewer copy; review-layout "does not mirror"; review-orchestrator Wave D (offset text into SKILL.detail.md to stay ≤ ceiling); flow-orchestrator, job-orchestrator, review-pr-feedback, feature-dev, task-implementer handling of held findings and follow-up sources; exempt lists, count tests, ceilings.
+- **T4 verify**: synthetic eval — a fixture reproducing the case (a timeline with an explicit `dir="ltr"`, an exemption comment and a sibling media control doing the same) plus control findings that are real; run `review-premise` live (Opus) and record verdicts; replay #992/#1005 ground-truth findings and record that none is challenged. Results in `eval/`.
+- **T5 review** of the PR, T6 docs/CHANGELOG, then release 0.3.121.

 ## Status Updates

When the scope touches UI, a store, or other code that holds state across events, `plan.md` carries a state × event matrix before `flow freeze`. Rows are the states the surface can be in (for example loading, loaded, empty, missing, first-load failed, refresh failed); columns are the events that reach it (for example the user switches selection, unmount, workspace or context change, retry). Each cell is one line: what the user sees and which state survives, citing the project's styling/UX rules where they decide it. Every non-trivial cell gets an `ACn` row, or one AC per group of cells with the same result; a cell that is genuinely "no change" needs none. List only the states and events the change reaches:
 
 | state \ event | user switches selection | unmount | retry |
 |---|---|---|---|
 | loading | drop the stale response; loading shows for the new one | no state write after unmount | — |
 | refresh failed | keep loaded data; the error does not follow to the new selection | — | re-fetch; error stays inline until success |
 
 It does not apply when the scope holds no UI or state (CLI output, pure functions, docs, build config): write `State × event matrix: not applicable — <why>` in `plan.md`. The matrix is what workers and fix rounds check behavior against; a choice no cell decides is a `behavior_changes` entry for the operator (Phase 2).
 
 ### A verification step in the plan is a task, not a sentence
 
 Every check the plan says must happen before the work is accepted - run the thing end to end, confirm two components agree, exercise the path no test covers - is added with `keryx flow task add` and closed with `keryx flow task done`. Prose in `plan.md` blocks nothing, and an orchestrator that wrote the step is the same one deciding whether to run it.
 
 The failure this prevents is specific and has happened: a plan listed "confirm both components agree on the same input" as step 5, the implementation shipped without it, and review found that the two did not agree at all - the change could not work in production. The check had been identified correctly and then skipped, because nothing made skipping it visible.
 
 Tasks are the mechanism for this. `keryx flow complete` runs a `tasks` gate over them, so an unrun verification step keeps the flow open instead of being quietly dropped.
 
 Know the gate's exact scope, because for years this file claimed a gate that did not exist and 24 completed flows shipped with an open task:
 
-- the gate is **opt-in per flow package**, keyed on `gates.tasks` in
-  `flow.json`, which `keryx flow init` writes for every flow it creates. A
-  package created before the gate landed does not carry the flag, and for it
-  the gate reports `skipped` and blocks nothing;
-- a task fails the gate when its status is not `done`; when its disposition is
-  `failed`; when its disposition is `blocked` (terminal, but the work did not
-  happen — and the harness emits this disposition on its own for a run that
-  ended blocked); when its disposition is `skipped` with no recorded reason; or
-  when its disposition is a value this build does not recognise. An
-  unrecognised disposition FAILS rather than falling through: a gate whose
-  default for the unknown case is "pass" is not a gate;

 ## Red Flags
 
 Stop and re-read this skill if you are thinking:
 
 | Rationalization | Rebuttal |
 |---|---|
 | "The worker's reply reads like it finished, so the task is done." | The STATUS protocol says read the `STATUS:` line first and never infer the outcome from prose. A reply without one is `NEEDS_CONTEXT` — a confident-sounding summary is exactly what an unusable result looks like. |
 | "`DONE_WITH_CONCERNS` is still done, so I can move on." | Every concern goes into `journal.md` and gets an explicit continue-or-fix decision before `flow task done`. Concerns dropped at the task boundary are invisible by the completion report, which is where they would have mattered. |
 | "The acceptance criterion no longer matches what we built, so I'll reword it." | Frozen AC changes only through `keryx flow ac update <id> --reason "<why>"`, or `--criterion ACn --text "<criterion>" --reason "<why>"` to rewrite the line itself. Rewriting a criterion to fit the implementation makes the flow pass a gate it actually failed, and leaves no record that it moved. |
 | "`flow.json` is just a file — editing one field is faster than the CLI." | `flow.json`, status transitions, task status and attempt counts are CLI-owned. A hand-written field desynchronises the durable state from the flow's own history, and the CLI's next gate check reads yours, not reality. |
 | "Tests pass and the review is clean, so I'll open the PR and complete the flow." | Phase 4 stops and asks the user how the flow should end; not every flow wants a PR. And completion requires a confirmed merge into the base branch captured at creation — not a green local run. |
 | "The worker returned BLOCKED twice — faster if I implement this task myself." | The implementer never self-accepts and the orchestrator never implements. Block the flow, escalate one concise question, then unblock and re-dispatch. Doing the work here erases the boundary the whole flow model rests on. |
 | "Verification is described in the plan, so it will happen." | A verification step in the plan is a task, not a sentence. If it is not a task with a status, nothing records whether it ran, and the flow reaches `implemented` with an unrun gate. |
 | "The review fan-out is cheap, so the budget check can wait." | `keryx review budget --spent … --outstanding …` gates the fan-out, and `review-orchestrator` runs inline in this same main session, where keryx cannot see the in-flight subagents; declare them with `--outstanding`. Skipping the check means the cap bounds nothing. |
 | "The reviewer wrote the fix; applying it is the fastest close." | A `suggested_fix` is a hypothesis. Most majors in a long fix loop are introduced by fixes: reproduce the finding red, check the suggestion against the state × event matrix, then fix (Phase 3 step 6). |
+| "The finding came from a review, so its premise is settled." | A finding can reproduce and still not be a defect. Never pass a held finding in `fix_context.review_feedback`; ask the operator and record it with `review decide-premise` (Phase 3 step 6); a flow sourced from a finding runs `review-premise` before freeze (Phase 1). |

 | "The implementer journaled its UX choice, so it is decided." | A `behavior_changes` entry with `needs_operator: true` is decided by the operator, asked with options before the result is accepted (Phase 2). A journal line decides nothing. |
 | "I'll set the verification kind later." | An `unclassified` criterion cannot become data afterwards without a recorded rewrite: `keryx flow ac update <id> --criterion ACn --text "…" --reason "<why>"`. Put the `[verify: …]` marker on every criterion before `flow freeze`. |

Three is the self-fix bound `task-implementer` and this skill share
 (`flow-orchestrator`'s review bound is five, by operator decision). *"The first three to four repair iterations account for
 most achievable gains"* ([arXiv:2607.05197](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05197));
 correctness falls **0.820 -> 0.673** across two forced revisions while
 cumulative ever-correct is **0.847**
 ([arXiv:2607.24604](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24604)). Other agent tools
 hardcode the same bound (`max_reflections = 3`).
 
 The bound is a ceiling, not a target. Repetition ends the loop earlier and
 **regardless of remaining iterations** — a counter cannot tell "converging
 slowly" from "stuck", and an agent emitting the identical failing output three
 times spends the whole budget before anything notices.

 ### Frontend / MobX laws
 
 These say what is **always reported**. What severity each carries is the
 conditions table under Finding Format, and it is the canonical rubric applied —
 not a second opinion.
 
 1. **Every observable mutation outside an action or `runInAction` is reported.**
    No exception for "small stores" or "simple assignments".
 2. **Missing `observer()` on a component that reads MobX observables is
    reported.** The component will not react to state changes — a silent runtime
    correctness bug, and silence is exactly why nobody else will find it.
 3. **An API call in a component is reported.** API/IO belongs in private store
    methods, not in JSX, hooks, or event handlers within the component file.
 4. **`public` on a class member is reported.** The ESLint rule

 - [ ] `ps-*` / `pe-*` / `ms-*` / `me-*` flip under RTL: an offset toward the start in

+- [ ] Some surfaces do **not** mirror, by platform practice (Material Bidirectionality,

On keryx shell with a large diff pass a small `--max-bytes` (for example 18000) and `--wave-bytes` (for example 54000) so no wave outruns a reviewer's five minutes; ledgers (csv, lockfiles, snapshots, generated files) are listed under `omissions` with a reason — list them in the report as not reviewed, never as clean.
 2. **Slices travel by path; on keryx shell, only by `context_files`.** The slices sit under the project (`<package>/slices`). On keryx shell pass each reviewer its slice paths in `spawn_subagent`'s `context_files`: the host copies the text into that reviewer's task, so you never paste or retype a slice. Elsewhere name the slice paths in the prompt. Put the `slices` ids in its reviewer-input. A dispatch that names a git range but no slice leaves the reviewer with nothing to read — that is `BLOCKED`, not a review.
 3. **Check before dispatch, every payload.** `keryx review dispatch-check --payload <file> --manifest <package>/slices/manifest.json --package <package>` for the wave; exit 1 means a payload names no slice, is over the wave ceiling (dispatch fewer slices, then the next wave), names a `skill_path` or `context_doc` that does not exist (`REVIEWER_INPUT_PATH_MISSING`), belongs to an unconfirmed over-threshold plan (`REVIEWER_INPUT_PLAN_UNCONFIRMED`), or breaks `reviewer-input.schema.json`. Fix it; do not dispatch around it.
 4. **One batch.** Dispatch the whole wave — up to 10 reviewers — in one message, not one at a time. On keryx shell every round reviewer's `spawn_subagent` carries `review_wave: {"package": "<package>", "pass": "round"}` (a wave outside it counts against the turn's 32 children) and a `timeout_ms` that fits its wave: the default 300000 is sized for a wave of 60000 bytes, so a larger `--wave-bytes` needs a larger `timeout_ms`. Give each reviewer `max_rounds` of at least 40 (the default); a reviewer that spends its rounds reading the skill and the schema returns nothing. **Incomplete means the next wave while it makes progress, Not run when it stalls.** Every reviewer result lists the `slices` it covered, in its `REVIEW_RESULT` object, as ids (`"slices": ["slice-01", "slice-02"]`); an object with an `id` and an optional `coverage` note (`{"id": "slice-01", "coverage": "read in full"}`) is read the same way. An object with a `status` counts only when it is DONE, COMPLETE, COVERED or OK (any case); a slice marked NOT_READ, INCOMPLETE, SKIPPED or PARTIAL is not covered, so give a slice you did not read no `status` of that kind and leave it out. An entry with no id counts for nothing. **One driver file per dispatch.** Write `<package>/drivers/<reviewer>.json` with `{"reviewer": "<name>", "slices": [<ids dispatched>], "result": "raw/<reviewer>.txt", "definition": "<path of the reviewer's SKILL.md>"}`: `ledger build` takes the reviewer's rule file from `definition` (a `skill_path` there, or inside a `payload` object, is read too) and the slices it was handed from `slices`. Only reviewer replies belong in `raw/`; a verification payload or a note filed there is reported as set aside and left in place, but it still costs a step. On `INCOMPLETE`, `BLOCKED` or `NEEDS_CONTEXT` (never accepted as a finished scope), and on a `DONE` that left slices open, `keryx review retry-plan --manifest <package>/slices/manifest.json --result <package>/raw/<reviewer>.txt --package <package>` decides and hands out the next wave of only the slices still uncovered (`--next-wave` plans one without a result). A result that covered a new slice spends no attempt; two results in a row with nothing new, or six failed rounds, print the `- **Not run:** …` line to paste into the report, and a result with nothing new first has its open slices cut in half. `keryx review slice --package <package>` already wrote one driver per reviewer x wave (`drivers/<reviewer>-w<n>.json`: slice ids, absolute slice paths, `result` path; the dispatcher adds `model`). Dispatch each wave in one batch, save each reply to its driver's `result`, and after each batch run `keryx review next --package <package>` (never `retry-plan` once per reviewer): it returns every reviewer's next wave at once, with reason `missing`, `retry`, `stalled` or `escalated`, or `done`. After a crash or timeout run it first: it collects late results from `<package>/raw/` and never re-hands a finished slice. Only the operator can accept a smaller set than that (`review_override_reviewers`, or `keryx review override-reviewers` in their terminal). An unfinished reviewer is never counted as a clean pass. **Persist every result, on every host.** On keryx shell pass each reviewer `save_result_to: <package>/raw/<reviewer>.txt`: the host writes its full final text there. Elsewhere the prompt tells the reviewer to write its whole reply to `<package>/raw/<reviewer>.txt` before it answers. Either way `review complete` has raw evidence after the transcript is cut, and you parse that file, never the tool output. Build `research.json` with `keryx review ledger build --package <package>` — never by hand: it reads the saved results, `scope-files.json` and the retry state, marks a reviewer complete only when its result is finished and its payloads cover the scope, and prints each gap with the exact next command and the waves left (a `retry-plan --next-wave` call, or a `--dispositions` entry for a raw finding). Run `keryx review ingest --research <package>/research.json` once it prints READY (exit 0). A refused `review complete` names what is missing: fix that with a command and run it again; it is never `blocked`. `--head` wants a SHA (`git rev-parse HEAD`), not `HEAD`.
 5. **Never print a scope or a slice.** The tool output of one call is cut at about 20 KB and `keryx review scope` of a large PR prints hundreds of KB. Run it as `keryx review scope --ref <base> --json > .metaproject/data/review/scope.json` and read the counts from the file (`keryx ctx read`, or `jq`); take `<base>` from `git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, not a guessed `origin/main`. Create `.metaproject/data/review/` first (`mkdir -p`) — a missing directory is a command to run, not a blocker. **Machine artifacts by direct write.** Save slices, payloads and results by redirection or `keryx ctx run --raw -- <command>`; the summarized form of `keryx ctx run` drops the bytes a later step parses.
 6. **Write mutants whole.** A testing reviewer's `mutant_candidates` cover every changed branch, code downstream of the diff included. Write them to `research-evidence/mutants.json` unchanged; you may not narrow them, and a candidate no pass has run still blocks the coverage gate (`SKILL.detail.md`, mutation pass).
 7. **Measure before `review-layout`.** Run the browser measurements (Playwright/Storybook) yourself and pass them in its first dispatch (`context_files` on keryx shell, by path elsewhere); they count as evidence when the command and viewport are named. A second `NEEDS_CONTEXT` from one role is Not run (`layout: no engine`), not another refill (`SKILL.detail.md`).

 ## Review Context Pack
 
 Before routing reviewers, build a compact `review_context` object. This is the shared source of truth for all sub-agents and must follow `.metaproject/skills/gdskills/review/review-orchestrator/review-context.schema.json`.
 
 Required content:
 - Request: raw user request, flags, review mode, explicit paths or commit range.
 - Git/PR metadata: repo, branch, base, head, merge-base, PR number/URL when available.
 - Scope summary: changed files grouped by domain, high-risk files, generated/ignored files.
 - Requirements: issue URL, linked task docs, acceptance criteria extracted from `context_doc` when available.
 - **The PR's own description**, fetched not assumed: `gh pr view <n> --json title,body`, into the typed `pr.body`. See below.
 - **Cross-repo contracts the diff depends on**, in the typed `cross_repo`: each pinned to the ref you read it at, and each recording whether the producer has merged. See below.
 - Rules: matched repository rules and convention docs by path.
 - **Memory: accepted project memory intersecting the changed paths.** See below — this step is required, not best-effort.
 - Decisions: why each reviewer was selected or skipped.
 - Token policy: effective budget, truncation decisions, files summarized instead of fully inlined.
 - Legacy/profile reviewer availability and selection state.

 ### Path gate — the second filter, same asymmetry
 
 Stack scoping asks *does this repository have the thing*. The path gate asks *does
 this diff*. A reviewer whose path triggers match **no file in scope A** is not
 dispatched; it goes to `Skipped reviewers` with reason `no-matching-paths`.
 
 This is worth its own step because `--all` is the common case and it is where the
 waste is: a run of sixteen reviewers over a fourteen-file frontend diff dispatched
 `review-core-boundaries` and `review-flow-graph` against a diff containing no
 `src/core/**` file at all. Two agents, full prompt each, guaranteed empty.
 
 Three bounds keep it from deleting coverage:
 
 - **Only path-triggered reviewers.** A reviewer selected by an explicit flag, or
   one whose scope is the whole change rather than a path set — `review-logic`,
-  `review-regression`, `review-verifier` — is never path-gated. One exception, for project reviewers only: a flag that more than one project reviewer carries is a **family flag** (the inventory lists it in that reviewer's `familyFlags`). It selects the whole family, and each member stays path-gated — `--<family>` over a diff touching one member's paths dispatches that member, not all of them.
+  `review-regression`, `review-verifier`, `review-premise` — is never path-gated. One exception, for project reviewers only: a flag that more than one project reviewer carries is a **family flag** (the inventory lists it in that reviewer's `familyFlags`). It selects the whole family, and each member stays path-gated — `--<family>` over a diff touching one member's paths dispatches that member, not all of them.
 - **Scope A only.** Scope B is the blast radius; it is *supposed* to name files the
   diff never touched.
 - **Ambiguity includes.** If you cannot decide whether a path matches, dispatch.
   Same asymmetry as stack scoping: a needless reviewer costs tokens, a missing one
   costs a defect.
 
 Record every gated reviewer with the trigger set that found nothing. "Skipped:
 no matching paths" is a result the reader can check; an absent reviewer is not.

 **Run this FIRST, before dispatching quality reviewers, whenever the change has a
 stated intent — an `issue_url`, a task doc, or a PR body.**

 ### Wave C — verification, and what it replaced
 
 Wave C replaced `review-strict`, a meta-pass that re-read the findings and adjusted severity with no new evidence. It was **removed, not improved**, on measured evidence:
 self-correction fell 95.5 → 91.5 → 89.0 (GPT-4, GSM8K) and 75.8 → 38.1 (GPT-3.5, CommonSenseQA), arXiv:2310.01798; Self-Refine's +49.2 on dialogue response generation is +0.2 on maths
 (arXiv:2303.17651), so re-reading helps subjective tasks and not verifiable ones. A verifier that **runs something** rejects most false reports.
 Do not restore the re-score because it looks useful. Full figures: `SKILL.detail.md` § "Why Wave C verifies instead of re-scoring".
 
 `review-verifier` occupies the slot and differs in one way that matters: it runs something.

- Pass the findings held when this pass starts (the whole consolidated set on the last pass), each carrying `global_id` and the **real**
   originating `reviewer`. A finding whose `reviewer` is the orchestrator cannot be
   routed away from its author, so the never-self-verify rule silently stops
   applying — that field was hardcoded to `review-orchestrator` on all 83 recorded
   findings and is fixed only from 0.2.70 onward.
 - **A finding is never verified by the reviewer that raised it.** When only one
   reviewer ran, its findings are simply left unverified; verifying them yourself
   is worse than not verifying them. The merge compares the two names after
   normalising case, surrounding whitespace, `_`/`-`, and a trailing `(model)`
   annotation, so `review-logic `, `Review-Logic` and `review-logic (sonnet)` are
   all the same actor. Do not try to route around it by respelling the name — the
   comparison deliberately over-matches, because a refused claim only ever costs a
   verdict while a missed self-verification costs the finding.

 | Rationalization | Why it is wrong |
 |----------------|-----------------|
 | "I'll pick the reviewers myself, by feel" | The set is what `keryx review required` prints, routed per slice; adding by feel over-reviews and dropping one needs the operator's own override |
 | "Spec compliance can wait until after quality review" | Stage 1 gate exists because unimplemented requirements invalidate quality work |
 | "I'll deduplicate findings manually in my head" | Always normalize to [F-NNN] format before consolidation to avoid losing findings |
 | "The reviewer's own severity table said blocker" | There are no reviewer tables. One rubric, in **Severity (canonical)** above; a reviewer that ships one is the defect this replaced |
 | "It's a security/architecture finding, so it's a blocker" | Severity is the demonstrated outcome, not the domain that found it. `blocker` is exactly the four shapes |
 | "It will definitely break something eventually, so blocker" | Name the trigger and the outcome. Named → `major`. Unnamed → `info`. "Eventually" is neither |
 | "A strict re-read of the findings will sharpen them" | That pass existed and was removed: self-correction without new evidence measured 95.5 → 91.5 → 89.0 on GSM8K and 75.8 → 38.1 on CommonSenseQA. Run something instead |
 | "Three reviewers agree, so the finding is verified" | Consensus is not evidence. 80+ agents unanimously endorsed a vulnerability that did not exist; one empirical test killed it |
 | "The verifier suggested a higher severity, I'll apply it" | It cannot suggest one. A claim carrying a severity is discarded whole and the attempt is recorded |
+| "The verifier confirmed it, so the fixer gets it" | Confirmed means the fact reproduces, not that it is a defect. Wave D judges the premise; a held finding waits for the operator |
 | "This finding has no `verification`, so it can be dropped" | Absent means nobody checked. All 83 recorded findings are in that state; none of them is thereby wrong |
 | "Precision went up after the verifier landed" | There is no precision baseline to have gone up from. State stage counts: dropped, refuted, retained |
 | "I'll widen the blast radius, this change looks risky" | It is bounded because review quality decays with context: F1 0.65 at round 2 → 0.29 at round 10. Widening makes the later rounds worse, not safer |
 | "The blast radius came back empty, so nothing can break" | Empty and unresolved are different facts. The graph indexes code — a Markdown or JSON change has no radius at all, and the record says which one you got |
 | "The changed files are the same as last round, so scope B can be skipped on the final round" | The final round always recomputes. A fix landed in round 3 is the change; skipping means the certifying round checked the least |
 | "This scope-B file has an obvious naming problem, I'll report it" | Rejected in code: a naming problem is `minor` at best, and the floor is `major`. The set is under regression check, not under review — raise it under scope A |

 | "The verifier returned nothing, so I'll confirm the findings myself" | The orchestrator never verifies. No verdict means `unverified`, stated in the stage counts |
 | "The spec-gate finding is mine, so `reviewer: review-orchestrator`" | That name makes the finding unroutable in Wave C. File it under the reviewer that ran the comparison |
 | "Steps 8–10 are done, I'll tick them now and ingest later" | `completed` means the ingest record exists. A plan that runs ahead of the artifacts is how an unrun review looked finished |
 | "The user said publish, so I can post the comment" | That chose whether, not what. Show the rendered body and get approval of it before any GitHub write |
 | "I cannot spawn reviewers, so I will review it myself" | A review nobody dispatched is not the review the report names. Run `keryx review run --autonomous` (Preflight 1); at the depth limit output the `BLOCKED` line and stop |

### 9. Redundant API Calls
 
 - [ ] Same endpoint fetched multiple times in the same render cycle or component tree without caching
 - [ ] Two sibling components each fetching the same data independently instead of sharing state / lifting to parent store
 - [ ] `useEffect` with a dependency array that triggers refetch on every render due to non-primitive dependency (object identity)
 - [ ] Polling without deduplication when multiple component instances are mounted
 
 ### 10. MobX: Derived State Computed in Renders
 
 - [ ] Value derived from observables computed inline in a component: `const total = store.items.reduce(...)` — should be `@computed get total()` in the store
 - [ ] Filtered list recalculated in render: `store.items.filter(x => x.active)` — should be a `@computed`
 - [ ] Conditional format derived from observable in render instead of a computed getter

 ## Verification
 
 Report done only once all of these hold:

- `keryx memory search --status accepted` for a prior decision that already
   settled this question. A draft entry is a hypothesis, not project truth;
 - `gdwiki` when the comment is about domain behaviour, a business rule, or an
   integration contract rather than about the code's mechanics.
 
 Assign one verdict per comment:
 
 | Verdict | Meaning | Goes to |
 |---|---|---|
 | `valid` | The problem exists at the named site, at this SHA | the fix plan |
 | `valid-wider` | The problem exists **and** at sites the reviewer did not name | the fix plan, as one class covering every site |
 | `already-fixed` | It was true when written; a later commit fixed it | reply only, citing the commit |
 | `not-reproducible` | The named path or condition does not exist at this SHA | reply only, stating what was looked for |
 | `disagree` | It exists and is deliberate | reply only, citing the decision, wiki page, or memory entry |
 | `out-of-scope` | Real, unrelated to this PR | reply only, plus where it was recorded instead |
 | `needs-clarification` | Two or more readings lead to different changes | asked, never guessed |
 | `unverified` | Could not be established — no access, no reproduction, missing context | reply only, naming what was missing |

+# Review — Premise
+
+Wave D. A finding can reproduce and still be wrong. The verifier asks whether the fact a
+finding names is there; this judge asks whether that fact is a defect. It reads each
+finding on a clean context, judges it, and emits one premise claim per finding. Its inputs are the reviewer payload only; session memory and earlier conversation are not inputs.
+
+## The case this exists for
+
+A final review reported: *the playback timeline is pinned LTR — two components hard-code
+`dir="ltr"`, so the timeline does not mirror in RTL.* The fact was true and reproduced.
+The finding was still wrong. Platform guidance says media playback controls and their
+progress indicator do not mirror (Material Design, Bidirectionality; Apple HIG, Right to
+left), and the code carried three signals of a deliberate choice: the explicit override,
+a lint exemption naming that area a physical-LTR island, and a sibling media control
+forcing the same direction. The finding was implemented; two reviews of the fix checked
+only the implementation, and one of them filed the sibling as a follow-up instead of as
+evidence against the premise. Asked "is this standard practice?", a model refuted the
+finding in one turn. No role had asked.
+
+## Workflow
+
+```
+review-premise Progress:
+- [ ] Step 1: Drop every finding you raised yourself, and every finding below `minor`
+- [ ] Step 2: Per finding, read only its bare claim (title, file, quote) and the code there; form a view
+- [ ] Step 3: Collect intent signals at and around the site (see question 1)
+- [ ] Step 4: Answer the four questions
+- [ ] Step 5: Only now read the reviewer's problem, impact, evidence and suggested_fix; revise if they show something you missed
+- [ ] Step 6: Emit one premise claim per finding judged, and nothing else
+```
+
+The order of steps 2 and 5 is the point. A reviewer's argument read first anchors the
+judgement on it; the claim and the code read first let you see what the reviewer did not.
+
+## Input Contract
+
+| Field | Type | Required | Description |
+|-------|------|----------|-------------|
+| `findings` | array | yes | Canonical findings (`review-finding.schema.json`), each with its id, `reviewer`, `severity`, `file`, `quote`, `problem`, `suggested_fix`. In a delta round, only findings with no carried premise. |
+| `judge` | string | yes | Your own name. Recorded on the claims file. |
+| `source` | string | no | `round` (default), `follow-up-issue` or `external-comment`: where the findings came from. |
+| `branch` / `base_sha` | string | no | So `git log` and `git blame` read the change under review. |
+
+## The four questions
+
+1. **Intent.** Is the thing called a defect a deliberate choice? Look for an explicit
+   override (`dir="ltr"`, `!important`, a pinned version, a forced flag), a suppression or
+   exemption (a lint disable, a `@ts-expect-error` with a reason, an allowlist entry), a
+   comment or commit message giving a reason (`git log -L <start>,<end>:<file>`,
+   `git blame`, `git show <sha>`), and sibling code doing the same. A signal does not prove
+   the choice right; it proves someone chose, so the finding has to show their reason wrong.
+2. **Accepted practice.** What do platform guidelines (Material Design, Apple HIG, WCAG,
+   the framework's own docs), the language's idioms, clean-code principles and common
+   patterns say? Then the project's own rules, with their known exceptions. A project rule
+   applied where accepted practice makes an exception is not a defect.
+3. **Consistency.** Would the suggested fix make the system more consistent or less? A fix
+   that makes one site differ from siblings doing the same thing is evidence against the
+   premise, not a follow-up.
+4. **Fix soundness.** Would a senior reviewer reject the suggested fix? A fix that is wrong
+   for the platform usually means the premise is wrong too.
+
+## Verdicts
+
+| Verdict | Meaning | Must carry |
+|---|---|---|
+| `upheld` | The premise stands; the finding goes on unchanged. | — |
+| `downgraded` | A defect, but intent or practice shows it is smaller than reported. | `severity`, strictly lower and never below `minor`, and ≥1 `intent_signals` or `practice_sources` |
+| `challenged` | Evidence says it is not a defect. | ≥1 `intent_signals` or `practice_sources`, and a `question` |
+| `owner-decision` | A product choice the code cannot settle either way. | a `question` and ≥2 `options` |
+
+`challenged` and `owner-decision` **hold** the finding: it does not count as an open
+blocker or major, it is not sent to a fixer, and the verdict lists it as awaiting the
+operator, who answers with `keryx review decide-premise` (`uphold` or `dismiss`). You never
+dismiss. `upheld` is the normal answer: a finding with a trigger, an outcome, no intent
+signal and no practice source against it is upheld.
+
+## Iron Laws
+
+| Rule | Why |
+|------|-----|
+| **You can only lower or hold.** No new finding, no raised severity, no edit to a finding's text. | The merge builds the record from the original finding and takes only your verdict; a claim carrying more is rejected. |
+| **Never judge your own finding.** | The merge rejects a judge equal to the reporter (`self-judgement`). |
+| **Claim first, argument second.** | The case passed two reviews that read the fix's argument and never the premise. |
+| **`challenged` cites.** Each intent signal names its `ref` (`file:line` or a SHA) and what it says; each practice source names the guideline and section precisely enough to look up. | An uncited challenge is rejected and the finding stays as reported. Never invent a quote. |
+| **Never re-grade by the rubric.** Severity is the reviewer's and the verifier's call; a test gap, a surviving mutant or a minor stays as reported unless intent or practice shrinks it. | An uncited downgrade is rejected (`downgrade-without-evidence`). Minors matter: a finding you weaken is one nobody fixes. |
+| **Read-only.** Run nothing but `git log`, `git blame` and `git show`, and read files. | Executing is the verifier's job; this judgement is about meaning. |
+| **An external finding is held, never dismissed.** | A human asked; the operator answers them. |
+
+## Output Contract
+
+```
+STATUS: DONE | NEEDS_CONTEXT | BLOCKED
+```
+
+- `DONE` — every finding given was judged or explicitly left alone (yours, below `minor`).
+- `NEEDS_CONTEXT` — the code at a finding's site cannot be read; say which.
+- `BLOCKED` — the findings input is unreadable or carries no ids.
+
+Then one premise claims object. The orchestrator saves it unchanged as the file
+`keryx review ingest --premises <file>` reads:
+
+````text

+  "judge": "review-premise",
+  "model": "<model id>",
+  "premises": [
+    {
+      "finding_id": "LY-003",
+      "verdict": "challenged",
+      "intent_signals": [
+        { "ref": "src/player/TimelineSlider.tsx:150", "says": "explicit dir=\"ltr\" on the timeline root" },
+        { "ref": "eslint.config.js:42", "says": "exemption names this area a physical-LTR scroll/pixel island" },
+        { "ref": "src/player/MediaControls.tsx:81", "says": "sibling media control forces the same direction" }
+      ],
+      "practice_sources": [
+        { "name": "Material Design — Bidirectionality", "says": "media playback controls and progress do not mirror" },
+        { "name": "Apple HIG — Right to left", "says": "video controls and timeline indicators keep their direction" }
+      ],
+      "reasoning": "The fact reproduces, but LTR is the platform practice for playback and the code chose it three times.",
+      "question": "The timeline is LTR on purpose, as platforms do. Keep it, or mirror it anyway?",
+      "options": ["dismiss — keep LTR, as platforms do", "uphold — mirror the timeline"]
+    },

+    { "finding_id": "LG-004", "verdict": "upheld", "reasoning": "No signal of intent; the null path is reachable from the form reset." }
+  ]
+}
+```
+````
+
+Then a short markdown summary: counts per verdict, and for each held finding its id, the

+## Scope Boundaries
+
+| Concern | This skill | Use instead |
+|---------|------------|-------------|
+| Whether a finding is a defect at all | YES | — |
+| Lowering a severity, holding a finding for the operator | YES | — |
+| Whether a finding reproduces | NO | `review-verifier` |
+| Adding a finding, raising a severity, editing one | **NO** | a domain reviewer in a new round |
+| Dismissing a finding | NO | the operator: `keryx review decide-premise --answer dismiss` |
+
+## Red Flags
+
+| Rationalization | Why it is wrong |
+|----------------|-----------------|
+| "The fact reproduces, so the finding is right." | Reproducing proves the fact, not the defect. The case reproduced. |
+| "The reviewer's argument is convincing." | That is why you read it last. |
+| "A sibling does the same; that is a follow-up." | A sibling doing the same is a signal of intent, against the premise. |
+| "The project rule says X, so any deviation is a defect." | Check the rule against platform practice and its known exceptions first. |
+| "It is clearly wrong; I will mark it dismissed." | You cannot dismiss. Hold it with a question; the operator decides. |
+| "Challenge anything ambiguous, to be safe." | A held finding costs the operator a question. Without a cited signal or source it is upheld. |
+| "I will run the tests to be sure." | Read-only. Running something is the verifier's method, not yours. |

 ### Shared laws (every reviewer)
 
 1. **A claim of runtime harm with no reproducible path is `info`.** If you cannot name the input, call, or condition that reaches the code, you have an observation, not a finding. Report it as `info` and say what would settle it.
 2. **Never flag the theoretical.** The path you describe must exist in the code under review. Do not report a safe API because it could be misused, or a pattern because it is often wrong elsewhere.
 3. **One finding per class, not one per occurrence.** When the same shape appears at several sites, report it once and list every site. Ten findings that are one finding hide the other nine problems.
+4. **A deliberate choice is not a defect until its reason is read and shown wrong.** An explicit override, suppression or exemption, a comment or commit giving a reason, or a sibling doing the same is a decision: read its reason (the comment, `git log -L` or `git blame`, the sibling) before you report it, and report it only when you can show that reason wrong. A project rule is checked against accepted platform practice and its known exceptions before a deviation from it is reported.
 
 Severity levels are defined once, in `review-orchestrator/SKILL.md` → **Severity (canonical)**. This reviewer does not restate them: `blocker` is the four merge-blocking shapes named there and nothing else, and the `major`/`minor` boundary is the trigger-and-outcome test.
 
 ---
 
 ## Orchestrated Review Contract
 
 When dispatched by `review-orchestrator`, follow the provided `reviewer-input.schema.json` payload. Return a `REVIEW_RESULT` object compatible with `.metaproject/skills/gdskills/review/review-orchestrator/reviewer-finding.schema.json`, then a concise markdown summary. Keep findings evidence-based, include concrete `suggested_fix` for every blocker/major, and return `NEEDS_CONTEXT` instead of guessing when required context is missing.
 
 ---
 
 ## Finding Format
 
 ### Class scope — required for `blocker` and `major`
 
 Every `blocker` and `major` finding must carry `class_scope`: **every** site that holds the shape you found, and **how you enumerated them** — the grep or query you ran, or the guard that derives the set.
 
 A finding anchored to one `file:line` is a claim about one site. The recorded history of this repository is that a fix then repairs that site and leaves its siblings: one writer of five, one operator instruction of four, six readers of eight. Each was found by the *next* review round, which is why reviews here have run to seven and four rounds instead of one.

 ## [0.3.120] - 2026-10-16
 
 ### Added
 - **Review rounds 2+ review the delta.** `keryx review start` finds the previous round of the same target — local package, review packages merged into the base branch, keryx's own round block on the PR, other PR comments, the flow package — and splits the change since the previous reviewed head into FIX changes (logic, regression and the authors of the attached findings, plus the slice's normal routing; every attached finding gets a disposition) and NEW changes (round-1 treatment). Code unchanged since the previous round gets a second look by review-logic and review-security-code, or a full review when the previous round was weak. Every orchestrator gets this by just calling `review start`; round details land in `<package>/round.json`.
 - **A previous round counts only when it is ours:** our own login's round block on the PR, a completed package merged into the base, or a matching entry in the machine-local round registry (written at ingest, complete and publish). A package the PR committed itself, a draft, or another branch's package gives a full round with the old findings as context.
 - **`keryx review plan`** runs start, scope, blast radius, slice, required and estimate in one step and writes plan.json; **`keryx review next`** returns the next dispatches for the whole package (no per-reviewer polling).
 - `review publish` adds a hidden machine-readable round block (no raw quotes); `comments collect` reads it back.
 
 ### Changed
 - Duplicate findings from different reviewers merge at ingest with one severity (the verifier's when present) and `reported_by`; later waves get `known_findings`.
 - Overlapping reviewer lines (the frontend family, project overlays via `supersedes`) collapse to one per slice; the core roles are never removed.
 - Reviewers are read-only except the verifier and one testing reviewer with a time budget.
 - flow-orchestrator plans a state × event matrix for UI/store work, gates after the first green, asks the operator about user-visible tradeoffs (`behavior_changes`), treats a reviewer's suggested fix as a hypothesis, and sends one implementer when red probes exist; job-orchestrator, feature-dev and review-pr-feedback take the round from `review start` instead of re-reviewing the whole branch.
 - Reviewer results are parsed leniently (fenced JSON, wrapper keys, lists of one reviewer's results) with a precise refusal otherwise; `review slice --package` writes per-wave drivers with absolute paths; dispositions have one validated schema; drivers and results record the model.
 
 ### Fixed
 - `ledger build` finds the project root for flow-bound packages; `--skip` of a required reviewer needs an operator decision; ingest into an existing package defaults to its head and refuses a missing commit; findings on a path absent at the reviewed head are flagged `path_missing`.

Also copies the `<dir>/<name>.mdc` rules the skills cite from the overlay's `rules/`: a rule the project lacks goes to `.metaproject/rules/<dir>/<name>.mdc`; one whose reference is already answered by a file with other content, or a `core/` rule keryx ships under the same name, goes to the reference's project slot `.metaproject/rules/project/<dir>/<name>.mdc` (statuses `differs`, `imported-project`; `core/x.mdc` → `rules/project/core/x.mdc`), which a reviewer's reference resolves to first. `rules/core` is rewritten by `keryx init`, `keryx update` and the legacy-profile `keryx skills install` (the manifest form with `--target keryx-shell` skips an existing file it did not record unless `--force`); `rules/project` is written by none of them. A file lying directly in `rules/project/` answers only a literal `project/<name>.mdc` citation. Re-run it over an existing import to fetch only the rules. The security gate runs on every `SKILL.md` and rule while the import is planned, `--dry-run` included: a secret is redacted and the row says so, and a file with a prompt-injection finding is `refused` (`would-refuse` on a dry run), writes nothing and leaves the rest of the import going, unless `--allow-flagged` is passed after you have read it (see [`skills import`](#skills)). That holds with the security module disabled too (the import runs the injection detector itself). A rule cited only by refused packages is not written (`skipped — cited only by a refused package`). A real run with any `refused` row prints every row and exits `1`; a dry run exits `0`. Undo with `keryx skills remove review/<name>`. |

 ### `review run` {#review-run}
 
 ```text
 keryx review run --autonomous --target pr --ref <pull request URL>
                  [--budget-minutes N] [--budget-tokens N] [--stall-minutes N]
                  [--out <dir>] [--provider p] [--model m] [--no-notify] [--json]

 One review of one pull request with nobody at the keyboard, in the `review-autonomous` profile
 (`keryx shell --print` in `trust` mode under `--review-system review-auto`, source only). It needs no
 terminal. It starts the review package, dispatches the reviewers, ingests their findings and closes
 the package with `review complete`.

keryx review tier --scope blast-radius --findings 12 --diff-lines 340 --json
 ```
 
 It sits beside `review scope`, `review blast-radius` and `review budget` for the
 same reason those exist: all four are *compute this mechanically, before
 dispatching, instead of eyeballing it*. The rule used to say an orchestrator
 "calls `decideDispatchModel`" — but an orchestrator is an agent following prose
 and cannot call a TypeScript function, so what actually happened was a model
 reading a table of signals and doing the arithmetic in its head. This is the
 entry point that removes that step.
 
 | Flag | Description |
 |---|---|
 | `--scope <scope>` | The round's scope. `blast-radius` floors the tier at `deep`. |
 | `--fix-attempt <n>` | 1-based attempt at the **same** finding. `>= 2` raises one tier. |
 | `--forced-strategy-change` | A strategy change forced by hitting the loop cap. Floors at `deep`. |
 | `--findings <n>` | Findings in scope for this dispatch. |
 | `--diff-lines <n>` | Changed lines in the diff under review. `<= 3` findings **and** `<= 50` lines allow `light`. |
 | `--verifier <method>` | `execution`, `site-check` or `reasoning`. The first two allow `light`: the evidence comes from running something. An unrecognised method is refused, not ignored. |
 | `--security` | Any security finding in scope. Never below `standard`. |
+| `--premise` | The dispatch is the `review-premise` judge. Floors at `deep`, beating a `light` verifier method: the judge reasons about practice and intent instead of running something. |
 | `--session-provider <id>`, `--session-model <id>` | The session's own provider/model. Omitted, they come from `KERYX_SESSION_PROVIDER`/`KERYX_SESSION_MODEL`; with neither, the block is adaptive. |
 | `--from-shell-config` | Use the selection `keryx shell` persisted as the session. Off by default: it is `keryx shell`'s last choice, not the caller's model. |
 | `--catalog <file\|->` | The candidate set, in the `detectProviders()` shape `[{"name": …, "models": [ … ]}]`. Omitted, providers are detected live. |

 Floors are applied after downgrades, so *at least `deep`* means at least: a
 blast-radius round over a twelve-line diff is still a blast-radius round. The
 output carries the ordered rule ids that produced the tier, so the answer can be
 explained afterwards rather than re-derived.
 
 **No model name exists in this command, and there is no `--tier` flag.** The
 session's provider/model and the candidate set are both discovered at runtime;
 `src/gdskills/model-tier.ts` places the tier relative to the session's own model
 using size words in model names (`mini`, `haiku`, `pro`, `opus`, …), never a list
 of models that exist. Accepting a hand-written tier would put the arithmetic
 back in the caller's head, which is the defect.
 
 **A model is named only when discovery found a different one; otherwise the block
 is adaptive, and exits 0.** With no session named, an unrankable catalogue, a
 session model carrying no size marker, or a tier that resolves to the session

`attach`, `start` and `ingest` accept the output of the `review-verifier` skill
 and merge it into the package. **The merge can only delete.** It cannot raise a
 severity, add a finding, or change a finding's text: the merged record is built
 from the finding as reported, and only the verdict is taken from the claim. A
 claim that carries anything else is discarded whole and the attempt is recorded
 in `scope.md`.
 
 This replaced `review-strict`, which re-read consolidated findings and adjusted
 their severity with no new evidence. That operation is measured to make accuracy
 worse — GPT-4 on GSM8K falls 95.5 → 91.5 → 89.0 across self-correction rounds and
 GPT-3.5 on CommonSenseQA falls 75.8 → 38.1 (Huang et al., ICLR 2024,
 arXiv:2310.01798) — so it was removed rather than improved.
 
 | Flag | Description |
 |---|---|
 | `--verifications <file\|->` | The verifier's result: an array of claims, or `{verifier, verifications}`. |
 | `--verification-mode <mode>` | `off`, `annotate` (default), or `filter`. |
 | `--scope <scope.json>` | The **whole** `--json` output of `keryx review scope`, so the record carries what the pre-filter dropped and why. Handing over only its `counts` object is refused: eight integers carry no reason for any individual drop. |
 | `--tokens-in <n>`, `--tokens-out <n>` | What the round actually used. Recorded on the package; absent means **nobody reported**, which is not zero. |
 
+### Premise — `--premises`
+
+`ingest` also accepts the output of the `review-premise` skill, run after the verifier over the canonical findings. A finding can reproduce and still be no defect: the code may carry an explicit override, an exemption note or a sibling doing the same, and accepted platform practice may support it. The judge answers `upheld`, `downgraded`, `challenged` or `owner-decision` per finding. **The merge can only hold or lower.** It never adds a finding, raises a severity or edits a finding's text, and it never dismisses one: `challenged` and `owner-decision` hold the finding for the operator, who answers with `keryx review decide-premise`. A held finding is not an open blocker or major, is listed as "awaiting operator", and fails readiness and the flow review gate until it has an answer.
+
+Claims that name an unknown finding, come from the finding's own reporter, challenge without a cited intent signal or practice source, or hold without a question (an `owner-decision` without at least two options) are discarded whole and listed in `scope.md`. Accepted claims are stored in `research-evidence/premises.json` and on each finding record.
+
+| Flag | Description |
+|---|---|
+| `--premises <file\|->` | The judge's result: the bare `{judge, model?, premises}` object, or a reply or report holding it in one fenced ` ```json keryx:premises ` block. A bare array is refused: it names no judge. |
+
 ### A finding points at the code it quotes
 
 A finding does not report a line number. It reports `quote` — the code it is
 about, copied out of `file` — and `review ingest` locates that quote at the
 commit the round records, writing the line the match started on. `line` is
 therefore **output**, and a number a reviewer puts there is overwritten.
 
 The reason is the failure it replaces: nothing compared a reported line to
 anything, so a number that had drifted travelled into `findings.json`, into the
 report, and into the disposition somebody later recorded against it. On a fix
 round the file has moved under the finding by construction, which is when the
 reported number is least trustworthy and most acted upon.
 
 Matching is exact first, then with whitespace collapsed, then it stops — nothing
 fuzzy. Three outcomes, all recorded in `locator`:
 
 | Outcome | What it means |
 |---|---|
 | `derived` | The quote was found; `line` is where, and `reported_line` keeps whatever the reviewer claimed. |
 | `unlocatable` | It was not, and `line` is `null` rather than a number nobody checked. The `reason` says which: the file is absent at that commit, the quote does not appear, or it appears in more than one place. |

 The merge cannot raise a severity, add a finding, or rewrite one; a finding is

+## Ask whether the finding is a defect at all
+
+A finding can reproduce and still be wrong: the code may carry an explicit
+override, an exemption note or a sibling doing the same thing, and accepted
+platform practice may back it (media controls and timelines do not mirror in
+right-to-left layouts). The verifier cannot see that, because it checks facts.
+`review-premise` runs after it, on a clean context, and answers `upheld`,
+`downgraded`, `challenged` or `owner-decision` for each finding. Like the
+verifier it **can only hold or lower**, and it never dismisses anything.
+
+```bash
+keryx review ingest --report round7.md --ref round7 \
+  --verifications verifier-result.json \
+  --premises premise-result.json
+```
+
+`--premises` takes the judge's JSON, or a reply that holds it in one
+`` ```json keryx:premises `` block. A `challenged` or `owner-decision` finding is
+**held**: it is not an open blocker or major, it is not handed to a fixer, the
+verdict lists it as "awaiting operator", and readiness and the flow review gate
+fail until you answer. You decide it, at a terminal:
+
+```bash
+keryx review decide-premise --package .metaproject/reviews/round7 \
+  --finding LY-003 --answer dismiss --reason "platforms do not mirror media controls"
+```
+
+`--answer uphold` returns the finding to kept at its original severity;
+`--answer dismiss` records it `dismissed-incorrect` with your reason as the
+evidence. In keryx shell the agent asks you the same question as a
+`review_decide_premise` card. An agent's shell cannot answer for you: the command
+is refused without a terminal.

When the scope touches UI, a store, or other code that holds state across events, `plan.md` carries a state × event matrix before `flow freeze`. Rows are the states the surface can be in (for example loading, loaded, empty, missing, first-load failed, refresh failed); columns are the events that reach it (for example the user switches selection, unmount, workspace or context change, retry). Each cell is one line: what the user sees and which state survives, citing the project's styling/UX rules where they decide it. Every non-trivial cell gets an `ACn` row, or one AC per group of cells with the same result; a cell that is genuinely "no change" needs none. List only the states and events the change reaches:
 
 | state \ event | user switches selection | unmount | retry |
 |---|---|---|---|
 | loading | drop the stale response; loading shows for the new one | no state write after unmount | — |
 | refresh failed | keep loaded data; the error does not follow to the new selection | — | re-fetch; error stays inline until success |
 
 It does not apply when the scope holds no UI or state (CLI output, pure functions, docs, build config): write `State × event matrix: not applicable — <why>` in `plan.md`. The matrix is what workers and fix rounds check behavior against; a choice no cell decides is a `behavior_changes` entry for the operator (Phase 2).
 
 ### A verification step in the plan is a task, not a sentence
 
 Every check the plan says must happen before the work is accepted - run the thing end to end, confirm two components agree, exercise the path no test covers - is added with `keryx flow task add` and closed with `keryx flow task done`. Prose in `plan.md` blocks nothing, and an orchestrator that wrote the step is the same one deciding whether to run it.
 
 The failure this prevents is specific and has happened: a plan listed "confirm both components agree on the same input" as step 5, the implementation shipped without it, and review found that the two did not agree at all - the change could not work in production. The check had been identified correctly and then skipped, because nothing made skipping it visible.
 
 Tasks are the mechanism for this. `keryx flow complete` runs a `tasks` gate over them, so an unrun verification step keeps the flow open instead of being quietly dropped.
 
 Know the gate's exact scope, because for years this file claimed a gate that did not exist and 24 completed flows shipped with an open task:
 
-- the gate is **opt-in per flow package**, keyed on `gates.tasks` in
-  `flow.json`, which `keryx flow init` writes for every flow it creates. A
-  package created before the gate landed does not carry the flag, and for it
-  the gate reports `skipped` and blocks nothing;
-- a task fails the gate when its status is not `done`; when its disposition is
-  `failed`; when its disposition is `blocked` (terminal, but the work did not
-  happen — and the harness emits this disposition on its own for a run that
-  ended blocked); when its disposition is `skipped` with no recorded reason; or
-  when its disposition is a value this build does not recognise. An
-  unrecognised disposition FAILS rather than falling through: a gate whose
-  default for the unknown case is "pass" is not a gate;
